Ellie edged her chair closer to the grown-ups who were visiting in the kitchen. Grandpa, Grandma, and Aunt Lily had stopped by for a visit, and although she didn’t always understand the conversation, she loved to listen. She found that she learned a lot of things that way.

The topic this evening was about something related to church and that got her mind to thinking about singing during Sunday morning worship services. Although Ellie was only five years old, she very much loved to sing. She thought about the fact that her dear Grandpa was a song leader in their church and how much she liked when he led a song.

At Ellie’s church the song leaders all sat around a table near the center of the church. They took turns choosing a song and then leading it for the congregation. Ellie didn’t always know the songs that were chosen. They sang out of a little black hymnbook that had lots of songs with hard words and tunes she didn’t recognize. However, in the back of this little songbook was a section called “The Appendix” and here were hymns that were familiar to her and she was always pleased when a song was announced from that part of the book. Her favorite song was ‘Saviour, Like a Shepherd Lead Us’ and although she couldn’t read yet, she knew it was number eight. When that particular song number was announced on a Sunday morning, she always felt a twinge of excitement. She would be able to help along with this song!

I wish we would sing that song again, thought Ellie. It’s been a long time since we have.

Then a sudden thought struck her. Why couldn’t she ask Grandpa to choose that song next Sunday?

Yes, I will ask him and see what he says about that idea, she smiled to herself. She decided to wait until her grandparents were ready to leave. She followed Grandpa out the door and as he walked across the porch, she quickly stepped up next to him. “Grandpa,” she asked. “Do you think you could lead the song ‘Saviour, Like A Shepherd Lead Us’ this next Sunday? I would really like to sing it again!” She felt suddenly shy at having asked such a question, and she ducked back toward the doorway of the house.

Grandpa smiled down at her. “I think I can do that. Is that a song you like?” His eyes twinkled at Ellie. “I’ll be happy to lead that one just for you.”

Ellie could scarcely wait for church the following Sunday. She would get to sing “her” song. Grandpa said he would choose it and she had no doubt he would do as he said.

Sunday morning, she waited eagerly for the song service to begin. The first and second songs were ones that were not familiar to her. Then came time for the third one. “Let’s sing number 8 in the Appendix,” announced the song leader. Ellie’s heart sang. They were going to sing her favorite song. Her grandpa had honored her request. Her eyes shone as she joined in the singing of the beautiful song. It was a lovely hymn that spoke of Jesus’ care as a Shepherd and a Friend, and how He would always keep His children close to Himself.

Later, after church was over and they were on their way home, Ellie remarked to her mother, “Grandpa chose that one song, just like I asked him to!”

Ellie’s mom looked a bit startled. “You asked him to lead a song today? When did you ask him?”

“Yes, I did. The other evening when they visited, I asked him if he could lead it today and he said he would. And he did!” Ellie said with delight.

Mom had a strange look on her face, and she was quiet for a moment.

“Did you know that Grandpas weren’t there today? At the last minute they decided to visit elsewhere this morning for church.” Mom smiled tenderly at her little daughter. “It seems that God knew what a little girl’s heart was desiring and He led another brother to choose the song you like so much. That’s so amazing, isn’t it?” Ellie nodded. To think that Grandpa wasn’t even at church today, and still they sang her favorite song anyway! It gave her such a special feeling to know that Jesus cared for her that much.

Today, Ellie is a grown-up woman and now has children of her own. Whenever she thinks about how Jesus cares for all His children, she especially remembers how God cared about one little, five-year-old girl and the song she loved so much. As her mother said, and still does, “Of course God cares. He loves all the little children of the world!”

Saviour, Like A Shepherd Lead Us

Savior, like a Shepherd lead us,
Much we need Thy tender care.
In Thy pleasant pastures feed us,
For our use Thy folds prepare:
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Thou hast bought us, Thine we are.
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Thou hast bought us, Thine we are.

We are Thine, do Thou befriend us,
Be the guardian of our way.
Keep Thy flock, from sin defend us,
Seek us when we go astray:
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Hear, O hear us when we pray.
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Hear, O hear us when we pray.

Thou hast promised to receive us,
Poor and sinful though we be.
Thou hast mercy to relieve us,
Grace to cleanse, and pow’r to free:
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Early let us turn to Thee.
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Early let us turn to Thee.

Early let us seek Thy favor,
Early let us do Thy will.
Blessed Lord and only Savior,
With Thy love our bosoms fill:
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Thou hast loved us, love us still.
Blessed Jesus! blessed Jesus!
Thou hast loved us, love us still.

Dorothy Ann Thrupp

اقتربت إيلي من كرسيها حتى صارت أقرب إلى البالغين الذين كانوا يزورون في المطبخ. كان الجد والجدة والعمة ليلي قد مرّوا لزيارة، وعلى الرغم من أنها لم تكن تفهم الحديث دائماً، إلا أنها كانت تحب أن تستمع. ووجدت أنها تتعلم أشياء كثيرة بهذه الطريقة.

كان موضوع ذلك المساء يتعلق بأمر في الكنيسة، فانتقل تفكيرها إلى الغناء أثناء خدمات العبادة صباح الأحد. على الرغم من أن إيلي لم تتجاوز الخمس سنوات، إلا أنها كانت تحب الغناء حباً شديداً. فكرت في حقيقة أن جدها العزيز كان قائد ترنيم في كنيستهم ومدى إعجابها عندما يقود ترنيمة.

في كنيسة إيلي، كان قادة الترنيم يجلسون جميعاً حول طاولة قرب وسط الكنيسة. كانوا يتناوبون اختيار ترنيمة ثم يقودونها للجماعة. لم تكن إيلي تعرف دائماً الترنيمات التي تُختار. كانوا يغنون من كتاب ترانيم صغير أسود يحتوي على الكثير من الأغاني بكلمات صعبة وألحان لم تتعرّف عليها. ومع ذلك، ففي ظهر هذا الكتاب الصغير كان هناك قسم اسمه «الملحق» وبه ترانيم مألوفة لديها وكانت تشعر دائماً بالسرور عندما يُعلن عن ترنيمة من ذلك الجزء من الكتاب. كانت ترنيمتها المفضلة هي «المخلّص، كراعٍ قُدنا» وعلى الرغم من أنها لم تكن قد تعلمت القراءة بعد، كانت تعرف أن رقمها هو الثامن. عندما يُعلن عن ذلك الرقم بالتحديد صباح الأحد، كانت تشعر دائماً بوخز من الإثارة. سأتمكن من المساعدة في هذه الترنيمة!

أتمنى لو نغني تلك الترنيمة مرة أخرى، فكرت إيلي. لقد مر وقت طويل منذ غنائها.

ثم خطر ببالها تفكير مفاجئ. لمَ لا أطلب من الجد أن يختار تلك الترنيمة الأحد المقبل؟

نعم، سأطلب منه وأرى ماذا يقول عن هذه الفكرة، ابتسمت لنفسها. قررت الانتظار حتى يكون أجدادها مستعدين للمغادرة. تبعت الجد إلى الخارج وبينما كان يمشي عبر الشرفة، تقدمت بسرعة بجانبه. «جدي»، سألت. «هل تعتقد أنه يمكنك قيادة الترنيمة «المخلّص، كراعٍ قُدنا» الأحد المقبل؟ أود حقاً أن أغنيها مرة أخرى!» شعرت بالخجل فجأة من أن تطلب مثل هذا الطلب، فانحنت عائدة نحو مدخل البيت.

ابتسم الجد لها من فوق. «أظن أنني أستطيع فعل ذلك. هل هذه ترنيمة تحبينها؟» لامع في عينيه نظرته لإيلي. «سأكون سعيداً أن أقود هذه الترنيمة من أجلك فقط.»

لم تكُ بالنسبة لإيلي الكنيسة في انتظار الأحد التالي طويلاً. ستحصل على فرصة لغناء «ترنيمتها». قال الجد إنه سيختارها ولم تشك للحظة أنه سيفعل ما قاله.

صباح الأحد، انتظرت بفارغ الصبر بدء خدمة الترنيم. كانت الترنيمة الأولى والثانية غير مألوفتين لديها. ثم جاء وقت الترنيمة الثالثة. «لنغنِ الرقم 8 في الملحق»، أعلن قائد الترنيم. غنى قلب إيلي. كانوا سيغنون ترنيمتها المفضلة. لقد لبّى جدها طلبها. تلألأت عيناها وهي تشارك في غناء الترنيمة الجميلة. كانت ترجمة رائعة تحدثت عن رعاية يسوع كراعٍ وصديق، وكيف سيبقي أولاده دائماً قريبين منه.

لاحقاً، بعد انتهاء الكنيسة وهم في طريقهم إلى البيت، قالت إيلي لأمها: «اختار الجد تلك الترنيمة، تماماً كما طلبت منه!»

بدت أم إيلي متفاجئة قليلاً. «هل طلبتِ منه أن يقود ترنيمة اليوم؟ متى سألته؟»

«نعم، فعلت. في الليلة الأخرى عندما زارونا، سألته إن كان بإمكانه قيادتها اليوم فقال إنه سيفعل. وقد فعل!» قالت إيلي بفرح.

كان على وجه الأم تعبير غريب، وصمتت لبرهة.

«هل كنتِ تعلمين أن الجد لم يكن موجوداً اليوم؟ في اللحظة الأخيرة قرروا أن يزوروا مكاناً آخر هذا الصباح للكنيسة.» ابتسمت الأم بحنان لابنتها الصغيرة. «يبدو أن الله علِم بما تتوق إليه قلب فتاة صغيرة وقاد أخاً آخر إلى اختيار الترنيمة التي تحبينها كثيراً. أليس ذلك أمراً مدهشاً؟» أومأت إيلي برأسها. أن يفكر المرء أن الجد لم يكن حتى في الكنيسة اليوم، ومع ذلك غنّوا ترنيمتها المفضلة! لقد منحها ذلك شعوراً خاصاً أن تعرف أن يسوع يهتم بها إلى هذه الدرجة.

اليوم، إيلي امرأة بالغة ولديها أطفالها الخاصون. كلما تذكرت كيف يعتني يسوع بكل أولاده، تتذكر خصوصاً كيف اعتنى الله بفتاة صغيرة تبلغ من العمر خمس سنوات وبالترنيمة التي أحبتها كثيراً. كما قالت أمها وتقول دائماً، «بالطبع يهتم الله. إنه يحب كل أطفال العالم الصغار!»

المخلّص، كراعٍ قُدنا

المخلّص، كراعٍ قُدنا،
كم نحتاج لرعايتك الحنونة.
فلتُطعمنا في رعياتك الجميلة،
ولتُهيئ آواك لنا:
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
قد اشتريتَنا، فنحن لك.
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
قد اشتريتَنا، فنحن لك.

نحن لك، فارحمنا وتآزر معنا،
كن حارس طريقنا.
احفظ قطيعك، وادفع عنا الخطيئة،
وابحث عنا حين نحيد عن الطريق:
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
استجب، يا اسمعنا حين نصلي.
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
استجب، يا اسمعنا حين نصلي.

لقد وعدت أن تقبلنا،
فقيرين وخاطئين كما نحن.
لديك الرحمة لتخفف عنا،
والنِعمة لتطهر، والقدرة لتحرّر:
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
لنَتوجَّه مبكراً إليك.
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
لنَتوجَّه مبكراً إليك.

لنطلب رضوانك مبكراً،
ولنَعمل مشيئتك مبكراً.
أيها الرب المبارك والمخلّص الوحيد،
املأ صدورنا بمحبتك:
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
لقد أحببتنا، فحبنا دائماً.
يابسوع المبارك! يابسوع المبارك!
لقد أحببتنا، فحبنا دائماً.

Dorothy Ann Thrupp

Around the world, but particularly in the United States, people seem to value rugged individualism. People who demonstrate this character quality make their own way through life, asking nothing from others and expecting nothing.

I suppose that this idea relates back to the pioneers. These were men and women who trekked across the various new countries looking for a place where they could settle down and call home. There were few general stores and as much as possible they lived as self-sufficiently as they could.

While this may sound like a scenario that demonstrates strength, the truth is somewhat different these days. These days people use technology to deliberately create bubbles of isolation around themselves.

Many older people have found themselves increasingly isolated from friends and family. COVID certainly made this worse, but there were seeds of this seclusion that had been sowed long before COVID was ever heard of.

Isolation is Not a Natural State

Looking back to the Garden of Eden we can see that Adam was created before Eve. While there were lots of animals around, there was no true companionship for Adam. And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him … And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him –Genesis 2:18-20.

And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man –Genesis 2:21-22. Of course, this was the beginning of marriage, but the more important thing to see here is that it is not a normal state for humans to be alone. We desire companionship and not just the companionship of a pet dog or cat.

Isolation can lead to Despair

Perhaps there is no story that demonstrates so clearly the dangers of isolation as the story of Elijah. We know from the biblical book of I Kings, that Elijah was a fiery prophet of God.

He brought word from God to Ahab that there would be no rain and there was terrible drought for the next three and a half years. During that time, Elijah spent time in the wilderness and then with a widow in Zarephath.

The whole time, he was miraculously fed through God’s power, first by ravens and then through God’s provision of flour and oil to a widow, with whom he lived. Through God’s power, he raised the widow’s son to life.

Then came a time when he challenged the prophets of Baal to a match on Mt. Carmel and won a decisive victory for God. Miraculous fire descended from heaven in answer to his prayer. Truly, God was working great things in his life.

Very soon though, Elijah was running for his life into the desert. Jezebel had threatened his life and rather than trusting God, he fled to Mt. Horeb where he heard the voice of God.

When God asked him what he was doing there, Elijah replied, …I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: for the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away –1 Kings 19:10.

We can see here a big reason for Elijah’s weakness. He felt completely alone. God corrected Elijah’s incorrect assumption when He stated: Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him –1 Kings 19:18.

The fact that those men and women existed in Israel did Elijah little good since he didn’t spend time with them. Elijah’s isolation led him to weakness and despair.

The story of Paul comes to mind as well. The Apostle Paul was a man who seemed to have nearly limitless amounts of energy and an unquenchable zeal for the things of God, but his last letter to Timothy from prison revealed a man who felt very alone. Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee… –2 Timothy 4:9-11.

The Apostle was not abandoned. Other than Demas, they had not fled because they were afraid or ashamed of his bonds. He had sent many of his friends away to strengthen the church in various parts of the Roman Empire. Yet, Paul was still feeling isolated and needed the good Christian brothers, Timothy and Mark, to come and encourage him as he faced a martyr’s death.

Isolation is Physically Harmful

Studies have showed that isolation is linked to higher rates of high blood pressure, heart disease, anxiety, and depression. Older people who are isolated often show signs of mental decline and can experience worsening dementia.

Many times, as people age, they experience the deaths of loved ones. The loss of a spouse can lead older people to withdraw from others and to experience loneliness and isolation. This in turn often leads to rapid progression of the aging process.

Science does not fully understand it, but loneliness leads to increased inflammation and poorer immune function. This in turn can lead to lonely people getting worse infections and struggling to recover after such an infection.

While we think of these problems as those that primarily affect elderly people, they can affect younger people as well. In younger people, often loneliness doesn’t lead to memory issues, but it certainly can lead to things like depression, and it can make chronic inflammatory diseases much worse.

The Opposite of Isolation

If asked what the opposite of isolation is most people would probably answer “Companionship” or maybe even “Friendship”. There is another word which has a Christian connotation that is even better. That word is fellowship.

The Greek word translated fellowship in the New Testament is “Koinonia” and in the Bible it speaks of relationships that are founded on a shared love for God and for the church—a unity of belief and desire. Christian fellowship includes concepts like praying together, encouraging one another, and even suffering together.

I am afraid that many today find themselves in one of two dangerous situations. First, they may not be a member of any church congregation. While this may be unavoidable in certain mission outreach situations, it is not ideal, and most certainly it should not be a normal situation. At the very least it can create a sense of isolation, and at the worst it hinders many of the “one-anothering” Bible passages from being followed. We need fellowship, both to encourage us and to keep us accountable.

The second dangerous situation is that many believers, while members of a church, isolate themselves within that church. If you are a member of a large church congregation, it is easy to blend in and not develop relationships with others. This is just as harmful as not being a member of a church body. Too many people feel lonely, even when there are lots of people around.

Scripture makes it clear that we need a church body. Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching –Hebrews 10:25.

There are many people who have lives that are full of friends and acquaintances, but if they do not have a place where they receive fellowship, they are missing out.

When I see people in my office who are struggling with depression there are two things I always tell them to do for themselves.

First is to start exercising. There have been several studies that compared exercise to antidepressants and found that it had similar effectiveness to many of the commonly prescribed antidepressant medications. This doesn’t have to be really vigorous exercise, but it does need to be aerobic (enough to raise the heart rate) and consistent.

The second is to become active in a church congregation; it is not enough to just attend church. Having brothers and sisters to pray for someone who is struggling, to listen to the discouraging situations, and to encourage that person to a more vibrant walk with God is really helpful.

Unfortunately, when someone is struggling with depression, the last thing they seem to want to do is make the effort to be around other people, which contrary to their feelings, is counterproductive to changing the problem.

As we consider this, it should move us to reach out to those who we know are struggling with isolation.

When someone loses a spouse, they often have a lot of encouragement for the first several weeks, but we need to make certain that they continue to have an active presence in their lives in the months that follow.

For every man shall bear his own burden –Galatians 6:5, should not give us excuse to not obey God’s command to Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ –Galatians 6:2. The family of God is given no time limit on bearing burdens. There is only a mandate that as we see our brother or sister struggling, we are to help them, as we are able.

The blessing is that someday, when we are struggling, we will have men and women of faith around us to encourage us and to pray for us. We cannot carry these burdens alone. Together, we will reach the Celestial City.

Isolation comes for many reasons. Sometimes it seems to be a chosen way of life, as is the natural tendency of introverted people. Sometimes it is foisted upon a person due to deaths of loved ones or other significant losses. Either way, it is not a healthy place to live.

As we find ourselves in these situations, we need to reach out for fellowship. The family of God is there for us if we only reach out.

As we see others who are struggling, we need to extend to them the right arm of fellowship. As we do so, we may, through our small efforts, help someone emotionally, physically, and spiritually, simply by being a friend in a time of isolation.

Runt om i världen, men särskilt i Förenta staterna, verkar människor värdera hårdhudad individualism. Människor som visar denna karaktärsegenskap skapar sig sin egen väg genom livet, ber inget av andra och förväntar sig inget.

Jag antar att denna idé för tankarna tillbaka till pionjärerna. Det var män och kvinnor som vandrade över olika nybyggen på jakt efter en plats där de kunde slå sig ner och kalla hem. Det fanns få butiker och så långt det var möjligt levde de så självförsörjande som de kunde.

Även om detta kan låta som en situation som visar styrka, är verkligheten något annorlunda nuförtiden. Nu för tiden använder människor tekniken för att medvetet skapa isoleringsbubblor runt sig själva.

Många äldre har funnit sig själva alltmer isolerade från vänner och familj. COVID gjorde detta säkert värre, men det fanns frön till denna avskildhet som hade såtts långt innan COVID ens hördes talas om.

Isolation är inte ett naturligt tillstånd

Om vi ser tillbaka till Edens lustgård kan vi se att Adam skapades före Eva. Även om det fanns många djur omkring fanns ingen sann följeslagare för Adam. Och HERREN Gud sade: Det är inte gott att mannen är allena; jag vill göra en ränna åt honom, som svarar mot honom ... Och Adam gav namn åt allt boskap, åt himlens fåglar och åt alla fälts djur; men för Adam fanns ingen som svarade mot honom –Genesis 2:18-20.

Och HERREN Gud lät en djup sömn falla över Adam, och han sov; och han tog ett av hans revben och slutade igen köttet därom; Och revbenet, som HERREN Gud hade tagit av mannen, gjorde han till en kvinna och förde henne till mannen –Genesis 2:21-22. Detta var förstås början på äktenskapet, men det viktigaste att se här är att det inte är ett normalt tillstånd för människor att vara ensamma. Vi åtrår gemenskap och inte bara sällskap av en hund eller katt.

Isolation kan leda till förtvivlan

Kanske finns det ingen berättelse som så tydligt visar farorna med isolering som berättelsen om Elia. Vi vet från den bibliska boken Första Konungaboken att Elia var en brinnande Guds profet.

Han förkunnade från Gud till Ahab att det inte skulle bli regn och det blev en fruktansvärd torka under de följande tre och ett halvt åren. Under den tiden vistades Elia i vildmarken och sedan hos en änka i Sarepta.

Under hela den tiden blev han mirakulöst försörjd genom Guds kraft, först av korpar och sedan genom Guds försyn av mjöl och olja till en änka hos vilken han bodde. Genom Guds kraft uppväckte han änkans son till liv.

Sedan kom en tid då han utmanade Baals profeter till en duell på Karmels berg och vann en avgörande seger för Gud. Mirakulöst eld föll från himlen som svar på hans bön. Sannerligen arbetade Gud stora ting i hans liv.

Mycket snart flydde emellertid Elia för sitt liv ut i öknen. Jezebel hade hotat hans liv och istället för att lita på Gud flydde han till Horebs berg där han hörde Guds röst.

När Gud frågade vad han gjorde där svarade Elia: ...Jag har varit mycket förbittrad för HERREN Sebaots skull; ty Israels barn hava övergett ditt förbund, nedrivit dina altaren och med svärd fördrivit dina profeter; och jag, jag är ensam återkommen; och de söka mitt liv, för att taga det bort –1 Kings 19:10.

Här kan vi se en stor orsak till Elias svaghet. Han kände sig fullkomligt ensam. Gud rättade Elias felaktiga antagande när Han sade: Men jag har lämnat mig sju tusen i Israel, alla de knän som icke böjt sig för Baal, och alla munnar som icke kysst honom –1 Kings 19:18.

Det faktum att dessa män och kvinnor fanns i Israel gjorde föga nytta för Elia eftersom han inte umgicks med dem. Elias isolering ledde honom till svaghet och förtvivlan.

Berättelsen om Paulus kommer också i åtanke. Aposteln Paulus var en man som verkade ha nästan gränslösa mängder energi och en outsläcklig iver för Guds saker, men hans sista brev till Timoteus från fängelset avslöjar en man som kände sig mycket ensam. Sträva efter att komma till mig snart; ty Demas har övergivit mig, då han älskade denna nuvarande tidsålder, och är avreste till Thessalonike; Krescens till Galatien, Titus till Dalmatien. Endast Lukas är hos mig. Tag Markus och för honom med dig… –2 Timothy 4:9-11.

Aposteln var inte övergiven. Förutom Demas hade de inte flytt i rädsla eller skam över hans fängslanden. Han hade sänt många av sina vänner för att styrka kyrkan i olika delar av Romarriket. Ändå kände Paulus sig fortfarande isolerad och behövde de gode kristne bröderna Timoteus och Markus att komma och uppmuntra honom när han stod inför ett martyrium.

Isolation skadar kroppen

Studier har visat att isolering är kopplat till högre förekomst av högt blodtryck, hjärtsjukdom, ångest och depression. Äldre som är isolerade visar ofta tecken på mental nedgång och kan uppleva förvärrad demens.

I många fall, när människor blir äldre, upplever de att älskade går bort. Förlusten av en make eller maka kan leda till att äldre drar sig undan från andra och upplever ensamhet och isolering. Detta leder i sin tur ofta till en snabbare förlopp i åldringsprocessen.

Vetenskapen förstår det inte fullt ut, men ensamhet leder till ökad inflammation och sämre immunfunktion. Detta kan i sin tur leda till att ensamma personer får värre infektioner och har svårare att återhämta sig efter en sådan infektion.

Medan vi tänker på dessa problem som främst drabbande äldre kan de också påverka yngre människor. Hos yngre leder ensamhet ofta inte till minnesproblem, men den kan säkert leda till saker som depression, och den kan förvärra kroniska inflammatoriska sjukdomar.

Det motsatta till isolering

Om man frågade vad som är motsatsen till isolering skulle de flesta förmodligen svara ”sällskap” eller kanske till och med ”vänskap”. Det finns ett annat ord med en kristen konnotation som är ännu bättre. Det ordet är gemenskap.

Det grekiska ordet som översätts med gemenskap i Nya testamentet är ”koinonia” och i Bibeln talar det om relationer som grundar sig på en gemensam kärlek till Gud och till kyrkan — en enhet i tro och önskan. Kristet gemenskap innefattar begrepp som att be tillsammans, uppmuntra varandra och till och med att lida tillsammans.

Jag är rädd att många idag befinner sig i en av två farliga situationer. För det första kan de vara medlem i ingen församling. Även om detta kan vara oundvikligt i vissa missionsutåtriktade situationer är det inte idealiskt, och det bör absolut inte vara ett normalt tillstånd. Minst av allt kan det skapa en känsla av isolering, och som värst hindrar det många av Bibelns ”varandra”-passager från att följas. Vi behöver gemenskap, både för att uppmuntra oss och för att hålla oss ansvariga.

Den andra farliga situationen är att många troende, även om de är medlemmar i en kyrka, isolerar sig inom den kyrkan. Om du är medlem i en stor församling är det lätt att smälta in och inte utveckla relationer med andra. Detta är lika skadligt som att inte vara medlem i en kyrklig kropp. Alltför många känner sig ensamma, även när det finns många människor omkring dem.

Skriftens gör det klart att vi behöver en kyrklig gemenskap. Och låten vi icke försaka vår sammankomst, såsom några hava för vana; utan uppmuntra varandra, och det så mycket mer, då I se dagen nalkas –Hebrews 10:25.

Det finns många som har liv fulla av vänner och bekanta, men om de inte har en plats där de får gemenskap, går de miste om något viktigt.

När jag ser människor på mitt mottagningsrum som kämpar med depression finns det två saker jag alltid säger åt dem att göra för sin egen skull.

Det första är att börja motionera. Det har funnits flera studier som jämfört motion med antidepressiva och funnit att det hade liknande effektivitet som många av de vanligen ordinerade antidepressiva läkemedlen. Det behöver inte vara mycket våldsam träning, men det måste vara aerob träning (tillräckligt för att höja pulsen) och regelbundet.

Det andra är att bli aktiv i en församling; det räcker inte att bara gå i kyrkan. Att ha bröder och systrar som ber för en som kämpar, som lyssnar på de nedslående situationerna och som uppmuntrar personen till ett livligare vandrande med Gud är mycket hjälpsamt.

Tyvärr, när någon kämpar med depression, verkar det sista de vilja göra vara att anstränga sig för att vara omkring andra människor, vilket trots deras känslor är kontraproduktivt för att förändra problemet.

När vi överväger detta bör det röra oss att sträcka oss ut till dem som vi vet kämpar med isolering.

När någon förlorar en make eller maka får de ofta mycket uppmuntran de första veckorna, men vi måste se till att de fortsatt har en aktiv närvaro i sina liv under de följande månaderna.

Ty var och en skall bära sin egen börda –Galatians 6:5, bör inte ge oss ursäkt att inte lyda Guds befallning att Bär varandras bördor, och så uppfyll lagen om Kristus –Galatians 6:2. Guds familj har ingen tidsbegränsning för att bära bördor. Det finns bara ett bud att när vi ser vår broder eller syster kämpa, skall vi hjälpa dem, så gott vi förmår.

Välsignelsen är att en dag, när vi själva kämpar, kommer vi ha män och kvinnor i tro omkring oss som uppmuntrar oss och ber för oss. Vi kan inte bära dessa bördor ensamma. Tillsammans ska vi nå den himmelska staden.

Isolering kommer av många skäl. Ibland verkar det vara ett valt sätt att leva, såsom den naturliga tendensen hos introverta personer. Ibland påtvingas det en person på grund av död hos älskade eller andra betydande förluster. I vilket fall är det inte en hälsosam plats att leva på.

När vi befinner oss i dessa situationer måste vi sträcka oss efter gemenskap. Guds familj finns där för oss om vi bara sträcker ut handen.

När vi ser andra som kämpar måste vi räcka dem den rätta armen av gemenskap. Genom att göra det kan vi, genom våra små ansträngningar, hjälpa någon emotionellt, fysiskt och andligt, helt enkelt genom att vara en vän i en tid av isolering.

It’s been said that in the 1500s, after baptism, the Anabaptists lived an average of only 27 days. They were hunted and killed. They realized one thing—serving Christ would most certainly cost them everything. They forsook the comforts of easy living; they forsook it all. It could also have been a similar situation when Jesus walked on the earth, or shortly after He was killed.

…and he turned, and said unto them, If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. And whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple. For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish. Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace. So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple –Luke 14:25-33.

Jesus clearly asked His disciples to count the cost. And they must have counted the cost, for they faithfully gave all, including their lives, for Christ’s Kingdom. They realized they could have had the good things in this life; however, they also realized it would cost them the good things in the next.

Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution –2 Timothy 3:12. If we look at the promises which Jesus gave us in His Word about persecution, and then compare them with the lives of Jesus’ followers today, we might be confused. And rightfully so.

He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked –1 John 2:6. Jesus says we should walk as He walked, He also tells us that we need to follow Him.

How did He walk? We know that Jesus had no place to lay His head—this was how He wanted it. We know that Jesus could have chosen to live where and how He wanted. He was, in fact, in control of the whole world, yet He was despised and rejected by the world and its system. When He spoke, people wanted to lay their hands on Him; they wanted to kill Him. He was not a popular person; He had few friends. In reality, He didn’t fit in, and He didn’t last long. Three years after His ministry began, He was killed. …He was numbered with the transgressors –Mark 15:28.

What about His followers today? Are they walking how He walked? And if not, why not?

We read about the children of Israel going through the wilderness. They fought and overtook the cities in their paths, killing all in the process. We read many accounts about how God instructed the children of Israel to kill all of the enemy, even the women and children. The following is one such account of many.

So the LORD our God delivered into our hands Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people: and we smote him until none was left to him remaining. And we took all his cities at that time, there was not a city which we took not from them, threescore cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many. And we utterly destroyed them, as we did unto Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children, of every city –Deuteronomy 3:3-6.

We read accounts like this in scripture, and it can cause us to cringe. It is almost as if life itself was not important. Even in the New Testament, death doesn’t seem to be that big of a deal. People lived and people died.

The first week after we moved to Haiti, I was driving through the city. Suddenly, right in front of me I saw a man lying in the street. Blood ran down the road and pooled in a low spot—he was dead. I was shocked. But what shocked me the most was that no one seemed to notice. People by the hundreds busily walked around him, not even looking at the man—no one cared.

Over the next six years we saw many dead or dying people—it became a normal scene.

If that was how it was back in the Bible times, and it is still how it is today in many countries of the world, maybe we are the ones that are out of the norm? Maybe we esteem life higher than God does. Maybe we are among those that Jesus spoke of when He said—He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal –John 12:25.

In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return –Genesis 3:19. We were created out of the dust, and after a few short years, we return to the very same dust.

Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away –James 4:14. The Bible also calls our lives a vapor.

We all know what happens after that—the judgment, then eternity. So why do we care so much about this life? Maybe it is an American problem or a western problem.

It is obvious that Americans are looked upon as ‘more valuable’ than most other nationalities. If you are an American in a developing country, you are heralded as a king. If something happens to an American, it is quickly headline news. I once stood over the bodies of two murdered men. One of their close friends stood by, so I asked him how he was doing. He shrugged and said, “This is life”.

So why does life mean so much to us Americans? The answer is simple. We can obtain almost anything we want; money is easy to get, and we can live how we want. We can live in pleasure every day. We go to the store and buy what we want, when we want—we have it our way. This is just how it is; for most of us it is all we have ever known—the life of plenty. So how does this affect us?

This type of living makes it especially hard to ‘give all’ for Christ. It makes it difficult to obey Jesus’ command to …Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature –Mark 16:15. It makes it difficult to say with the Apostle Paul, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain –Philippians 1:21. In reality, it makes it difficult to be a Christian.

When Jesus said… For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25, what did He mean? Could it mean literally just what it says: that when you fall in love with your own life, you cannot effectively follow Christ, so that in the end you will actually lose your life?

Can you go to the lost and forsake the comforts of this life if it’s those comforts that you love and live for? It’s not likely. What we have is “Americanized” Christians that will only go to the mission field if they can take their comforts with them. This produces rich, comfortable missionaries who, despite their best efforts, can’t win the lost, rather they make them jealous. Can we go into the cities and preach the gospel to the lost like so many before us have? Can we take time to teach and disciple the tens of thousands who are seeking? If we love our lives, we probably will not, since there is too much to lose and it’s a waste of good talent and opportunity. God help us.

When we are living to please the flesh and we have our lives figured out, it is hard for God to use us. We are puffed up. We tend to believe that God has blessed us because of all our possessions and our status in life; but isn’t this the prosperity gospel? What if that changed? Would we still consider ourselves to be blessed? Is it God or our own doing that causes us to be joyful? What if we found ourselves in John the Baptist’s shoes? Or the Apostle Paul’s? If we would be sitting in prison for doing nothing wrong, would our joy remain? It should if the Holy Spirit is living and working in our hearts. The Bible says that we can suffer joyfully!

Years ago, a coworker of mine was a happy fellow. He had a nice life. There was one problem—he did not believe there was a God. We would talk day after day. He would constantly tell me how happy he was and that one didn’t need to be a Christian to be happy. He would talk about his nice life, all that he possessed, his good job, his nice family. Interestingly enough, he truly did seem happy.

I would tell him that true happiness didn’t come from the things that we possess or the position that we find ourselves in, but he would just disagree. He also proclaimed that he lived a better life than most Christians that he knew. He also said he didn’t get angry like most Christians and could control himself. I tried to convince him that he was deceived. At times I would think I was getting somewhere with him, then later it would seem I was far from reaching him. One day he soberly admitted that I seemed to be different that most Christians he had known in the past, but that still wasn’t enough.

I left that job and lost contact with him. Recently, I ran into another one of my former coworkers. I quickly thought of my friend and asked how he was doing. He looked at me strangely and then shocked me to my core as he said, “He committed suicide”.

The devil wants us to love our life—it’s that simple. When we love our life, we focus on it, we cherish it. The last thing we want to do is lose our life, even if it is for something eternal.

When I was in the Marines, they would constantly remind us that our lives were not number one; our country was. There are many young men who put their country first. Many have gone and given their all; many have died.

In World War 2, the Japanese would try to sneak up to a fox hole housing soldiers and throw in a grenade. Many times, it didn’t end like the Japanese wanted, because someone would jump on the grenade, absorbing the explosion. Thousands gave their lives to save their friends and defend their country. But be sure, if their priorities were not in order (of country first before themselves), they would not have done so.

If someone today, in America, would risk their life for the sake of the gospel, he would be labeled as foolish, reckless, and immature. But what do we say about so many before us—the ones that gave their lives while standing for the same things that we say we believe today? And what about the thousands today who are putting their lives on the line in other countries—are they foolish? Let’s look at a very obvious example in Acts.

And as we tarried there many days, there came down from Judaea a certain prophet, named Agabus. And when he was come unto us, he took Paul’s girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. And when we heard these things, both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. –Acts 21:10-13.

What would we think of Paul’s actions today? Paul went to Jerusalem and was quickly taken, beaten, and put in prison. It was the beginning of the end for our dear brother. He was moved from prison to prison and eventually ended up in Rome where he was beheaded. What do you think the ones that tried to persuade him to not go to Jerusalem thought? Do you think they called him a fool? Did they shake their heads and say, “I told him not to go!”?

We cannot know for sure. However, I am sure that Paul was simply putting the kingdom of Christ first; his life did not matter. He was obeying God, and God had told him to go.

When we love our lives, it is very difficult to be an effective disciple of the Lord Jesus. We end up forsaking God’s calling and then we are stuck trying to live the Christian life alone, and without God—no spiritual help from above, causing us to fall way short of the mark.

It’s ironic that only when we forsake all, including our lives, will we find true peace and purpose for our lives. And when we love our lives, that is when we will lose them.

Rise up, O saints of God!
Have done with lesser things.
Give heart and soul and mind and strength
To serve the King of kings.

Rise up, O saints of God!
The kingdom tarries long.
Bring in the day of Christlike love
And end the night of wrong.

Lift high the cross of Christ!
Tread where His feet have trod.
Led onward by the Son of Man,
Rise up, O saints of God!

Let us rise up, as God’s people, and begin to be done with lesser things, with our gaze on things above, not on the things of this earth. Yes, we will stand out; we will be labeled fools and many other things. However, we will once again catch God’s attention and the fires of revival will once again burn!

Si dice che nel 1500, dopo il battesimo, gli anabattisti vivevano in media solo 27 giorni. Venivano cacciati e uccisi. Comprendevano una cosa: servire Cristo di certo sarebbe costato loro tutto. Rinunciarono ai conforti della vita facile; rinunciarono a tutto. Potrebbe essere stata una situazione simile quando Gesù camminava sulla terra, o poco dopo che fu ucciso.

…e voltatosi disse loro: «Se uno viene a me e non odia il padre, la madre, la donna, i figli, i fratelli, le sorelle e anche la propria vita, non può essere mio discepolo. Chi non porta la sua croce e non viene dietro a me, non può essere mio discepolo. Poiché quale di voi, volendo edificare una torre, non si siede prima e non conta il costo, se ha con sé quanto gli occorre per terminarla? Per non avvenire poi che, avendo posto il fondamento e non potendo terminare, tutti quelli che vedono comincino a schernirlo dicendo: Costui ha cominciato a costruire e non ha potuto terminare. O quale re, andando a far guerra contro un altro re, non si mette prima a sedere e non considera se con diecimila può fronteggiare colui che viene contro di lui con ventimila? Per non succedere poi che, essendo l’altro ancora lontano, gli mandi un’ambasciata e gli domandi condizioni di pace? Così anche voi: chiunque di voi non rinuncia a tutto ciò che ha, non può essere mio discepolo» – Luca 14:25-33.

Gesù ha chiaramente chiesto ai suoi discepoli di contare il costo. E dovettero aver contato il costo, perché fedelmente donarono tutto, comprese le loro vite, per il regno di Cristo. Capirono che avrebbero potuto avere le cose buone in questa vita; però compresero anche che ciò avrebbe loro fatto perdere le cose buone nella vita che verrà.

Or tutti quelli che vogliono vivere piamente in Cristo Gesù subiranno persecuzione – 2 Timoteo 3:12. Se guardiamo alle promesse che Gesù ci ha fatto nella Sua Parola riguardo alle persecuzioni, e poi le confrontiamo con le vite dei seguaci di Gesù oggi, potremmo restare confusi. E a ragione.

Chi dice di dimorare in lui deve anche camminare come camminò lui – 1 Giovanni 2:6. Gesù dice che dovremmo camminare come Lui camminò, e ci dice anche che dobbiamo seguirlo.

Come camminò? Sappiamo che Gesù non aveva un luogo dove posare il capo—così lo volle. Sappiamo che Gesù avrebbe potuto scegliere di vivere dove e come voleva. Egli, infatti, aveva il controllo del mondo intero, eppure fu disprezzato e rifiutato dal mondo e dal suo sistema. Quando parlava, la gente voleva mettergli le mani addosso; volevano ucciderlo. Non era una persona popolare; aveva pochi amici. In realtà non si adattava, e non durò a lungo. Tre anni dopo l'inizio del suo ministero fu ucciso. …Fu contato tra gli empi – Marco 15:28.

Che dire dei suoi seguaci oggi? Camminano come Lui camminò? E se no, perché no?

Leggiamo dei figli d'Israele che attraversano il deserto. Combattevano e conquistavano le città sul loro cammino, uccidendo tutti nel processo. Troviamo molti resoconti in cui Dio istruisce i figli d'Israele a uccidere tutti i nemici, persino donne e bambini. Il seguente è uno di questi molti resoconti.

Così il SIGNORE nostro Dio diede nelle nostre mani anche Og, re di Basan, con tutto il suo popolo; noi lo colpimmo fino a non lasciargli più alcuno in vita. E in quel tempo prendemmo tutte le sue città; non ci fu città che non prendemmo di loro, sessanta città, tutta la regione di Argob, il regno di Og in Basan. Tutte queste città avevano mura alte, porte e battenti; oltre a questo molte erano città senza mura. E le distruggemmo completamente, come avevamo fatto al re Sicone di Ešnòn, distruggendo completamente uomini, donne e bambini, di ogni città – Deuteronomio 3:3-6.

Leggiamo racconti simili nelle Scritture, e questo può farci rabbrividire. È quasi come se la vita in sé non fosse importante. Anche nel Nuovo Testamento la morte non sembra essere così grave. La gente viveva e la gente moriva.

La prima settimana dopo che ci trasferimmo ad Haiti, guidavo per la città. All'improvviso, proprio davanti a me vidi un uomo sdraiato in mezzo alla strada. Il sangue scorreva lungo la via e si raccoglieva in una depressione—era morto. Rimasi scioccato. Ma ciò che mi scioccò di più fu che nessuno sembrava accorgersene. Centinaia di persone camminavano affaccendate intorno a lui, senza neppure guardare l'uomo—nessuno se ne curava.

Nei successivi sei anni vedemmo molte persone morte o morenti—divenne una scena normale.

Se era così anche nei tempi biblici, e lo è ancora oggi in molti paesi del mondo, forse siamo noi ad essere fuori dalla norma? Forse stimiamo la vita più di quanto faccia Dio. Forse siamo tra coloro di cui Gesù parlò quando disse—Chi ama la propria vita la perderà; e chi odia la propria vita in questo mondo la conserverà per la vita eterna – Giovanni 12:25.

Con il sudore del tuo volto mangerai il pane, finché non torni alla terra, poiché da essa sei stato tratto; polvere sei e in polvere ritornerai – Genesi 3:19. Siamo stati creati dalla polvere, e dopo pochi brevi anni torniamo alla stessa polvere.

Voi non sapete quel che accadrà domani; infatti che cos’è la vostra vita? È un vapore che appare per un poco e poi svanisce – Giacomo 4:14. La Bibbia chiama la nostra vita anche un vapore.

Sappiamo tutti cosa succede dopo—il giudizio, poi l’eternità. Allora perché ci importa tanto di questa vita? Forse è un problema americano o occidentale.

È ovvio che gli americani sono considerati «più preziosi» della maggior parte delle altre nazionalità. Se sei americano in un paese in via di sviluppo, vieni trattato come un re. Se succede qualcosa a un americano, è subito notizia in prima pagina. Una volta stetti vicino ai corpi di due uomini uccisi. Uno dei loro amici stava lì vicino, così gli chiesi come stesse. Lui scrollò le spalle e disse: «Questa è la vita».

Allora perché la vita significa così tanto per noi americani? La risposta è semplice. Possediamo quasi tutto ciò che vogliamo; il denaro è facile da ottenere e possiamo vivere come desideriamo. Possiamo vivere nel piacere ogni giorno. Andiamo al negozio e compriamo ciò che vogliamo, quando lo vogliamo—la nostra vita a modo nostro. È così; per la maggior parte di noi è tutto ciò che abbiamo mai conosciuto—la vita dell'abbondanza. In che modo questo ci influenza?

Questo tipo di vita rende particolarmente difficile «dare tutto» per Cristo. Rende difficile obbedire al comando di Gesù di …andate per tutto il mondo e predicate il vangelo a ogni creatura – Marco 16:15. Rende difficile dire con l'apostolo Paolo, Per me vivere è Cristo e per me morire è guadagno – Filippesi 1:21. In realtà rende difficile essere cristiani.

Quando Gesù disse… Chi vorrà conservare la propria vita la perderà; ma chi perderà la propria vita per causa mia la troverà – Matteo 16:25, cosa intendeva? Potrebbe significare letteralmente ciò che dice: che quando ti innamori della tua propria vita, non puoi seguire Cristo efficacemente, e alla fine perderai la vita?

Puoi andare verso i perduti e rinunciare ai conforti di questa vita se sono proprio quei conforti che ami e per cui vivi? Non è probabile. Quello che abbiamo sono cristiani «americanizzati» che andranno in missione solo se possono portare i loro conforti con sé. Questo produce missionari ricchi e a loro agio che, nonostante i loro migliori sforzi, non riescono a vincere i perduti; anzi suscitano la loro invidia. Possiamo andare nelle città e predicare il vangelo ai perduti come tanti prima di noi hanno fatto? Possiamo prenderci il tempo per insegnare e fare discepolato a decine di migliaia che cercano? Se amiamo la nostra vita, probabilmente non lo faremo, poiché c'è troppo da perdere e sembra uno spreco di talenti e opportunità. Dio ci aiuti.

Quando viviamo per piacere alla carne e crediamo di avere la vita sotto controllo, è difficile che Dio ci usi. Siamo gonfi di orgoglio. Tendiamo a credere che Dio ci abbia benedetto a causa di tutti i nostri possedimenti e del nostro status nella vita; ma non è forse questo il vangelo della prosperità? E se ciò cambiasse? Ci considereremmo ancora benedetti? È Dio o è merito nostro se siamo gioiosi? E se ci trovassimo nelle scarpe di Giovanni il Battista? O in quelle dell'apostolo Paolo? Se ci trovassimo in prigione per non aver fatto nulla di male, la nostra gioia resterebbe? Dovrebbe se lo Spirito Santo vive e opera nei nostri cuori. La Bibbia dice che possiamo soffrire con gioia!

Anni fa, un mio collega era un uomo allegro. Aveva una bella vita. C’era un problema—non credeva che esistesse Dio. Parlavamo giorno dopo giorno. Mi diceva continuamente quanto fosse felice e che non occorreva essere cristiani per esserlo. Parlava della sua bella vita, di tutto ciò che possedeva, del suo buon lavoro, della sua bella famiglia. Sorprendentemente, sembrava davvero felice.

Io gli dicevo che la vera felicità non veniva dalle cose che possediamo o dalla posizione in cui ci troviamo, ma lui dissentiva. Proclamava inoltre di vivere meglio della maggior parte dei cristiani che conosceva. Diceva anche di non arrabbiarsi come molti cristiani e di saper controllare se stesso. Cercai di convincerlo che era ingannato. A volte pensavo di star ottenendo qualche risultato con lui, poi sembrava che fossi lontano dal raggiungerlo. Un giorno ammise seriamente che sembravo diverso dalla maggior parte dei cristiani che aveva conosciuto in passato, ma ciò non bastò.

Lasciai quel lavoro e persi i contatti. Recentemente incontrai un altro mio ex collega. Pensai subito al mio amico e gli chiesi come stesse. Mi guardò stranito e poi mi scosse fino al profondo dicendo: «Si è suicidato».

Il diavolo vuole che amiamo la nostra vita—è così semplice. Quando amiamo la nostra vita, ci concentriamo su di essa, la custodiamo. L’ultima cosa che vogliamo fare è perdere la nostra vita, anche se è per qualcosa di eterno.

Quando ero nei Marines, ci ricordavano continuamente che le nostre vite non erano la cosa principale; lo era la nostra patria. Ci sono molti giovani che mettono la patria al primo posto. Molti sono andati e hanno dato tutto; molti sono morti.

Nella Seconda Guerra Mondiale, i giapponesi cercavano di avvicinarsi furtivamente a una trincea che ospitava dei soldati e lanciare una granata. Molte volte non andò come i giapponesi avevano sperato, perché qualcuno si gettò sulla granata, assorbendone l'esplosione. Migliaia hanno dato la loro vita per salvare i loro amici e difendere la patria. Ma stai certo che, se le loro priorità non fossero state in ordine (la patria prima di se stessi), non l'avrebbero fatto.

Se qualcuno oggi, in America, rischiasse la propria vita per il vangelo, verrebbe etichettato come folle, spericolato e immaturo. Ma cosa diremo di tanti antesignani—di quelli che hanno dato la vita pur sostenendo le stesse cose che oggi diciamo di credere? E che dire delle migliaia oggi che mettono a rischio la loro vita in altri paesi—sono forse sciocchi? Guardiamo a un esempio molto evidente negli Atti.

Mentre restavamo là molti giorni, scese dalla Giudea un certo profeta, di nome Agabo. Venuto da noi, prese la cintura di Paolo, gli legò le mani e i piedi e disse: «Così dice lo Spirito Santo: così i Giudei a Gerusalemme legheranno l’uomo a cui appartiene questa cintura e lo consegneranno in mano ai pagani». Udito ciò, noi e quelli del luogo lo pregammo vivamente di non salire a Gerusalemme. Allora Paolo rispose: «Perché piangete e mi spezzate il cuore? Sono pronto non solo ad essere legato, ma anche a morire a Gerusalemme per il nome del Signore Gesù» – Atti 21:10-13.

Cosa penseremmo oggi delle azioni di Paolo? Paolo andò a Gerusalemme e fu presto catturato, percosso e messo in prigione. Fu l’inizio della fine per il nostro caro fratello. Fu spostato di prigione in prigione e alla fine finì a Roma dove fu decapitato. Cosa pensate che coloro che cercarono di persuaderlo a non andare pensassero? Pensate che lo chiamarono sciocco? Scossero la testa dicendo: «Te l’avevo detto di non andarci!»?

Non possiamo saperlo con certezza. Tuttavia, sono certo che Paolo stava semplicemente ponendo il regno di Cristo al primo posto; la sua vita non contava. Stava obbedendo a Dio, e Dio gli aveva detto di andare.

Quando amiamo la nostra vita, è molto difficile essere un discepolo efficace del Signore Gesù. Finiremo per abbandonare la chiamata di Dio e poi cercheremo di vivere la vita cristiana da soli e senza Dio—senza aiuto spirituale dall’alto, il che ci porta a rimanere ben al di sotto del segno.

È ironico che solo quando rinunciamo a tutto, compresa la nostra vita, troveremo vera pace e uno scopo per la nostra esistenza. E quando amiamo la nostra vita, è allora che la perderemo.

Sorgete, o santi di Dio!
Abbandonate le cose minori.
Date cuore e anima e mente e forza
Per servire il Re dei re.

Sorgete, o santi di Dio!
Il regno tarda a venire.
Portate il giorno dell'amore cristiforme
E finite la notte dell'ingiustizia.

Ergete alto la croce di Cristo!
Calpestate dove i suoi piedi hanno camminato.
Guidati dal Figlio dell'uomo,
Sorgete, o santi di Dio!

Sorgiamo, come popolo di Dio, e cominciamo a smettere con le cose minori, con lo sguardo rivolto alle cose di lassù, non alle cose di questa terra. Sì, ci distingueremo; saremo etichettati come sciocchi e con molti altri nomi. Tuttavia, attireremo nuovamente l'attenzione di Dio e i fuochi del risveglio bruceranno ancora una volta!

Around the world, but particularly in the United States, people seem to value rugged individualism. People who demonstrate this character quality make their own way through life, asking nothing from others and expecting nothing.

I suppose that this idea relates back to the pioneers. These were men and women who trekked across the various new countries looking for a place where they could settle down and call home. There were few general stores and as much as possible they lived as self-sufficiently as they could.

While this may sound like a scenario that demonstrates strength, the truth is somewhat different these days. These days people use technology to deliberately create bubbles of isolation around themselves.

Many older people have found themselves increasingly isolated from friends and family. COVID certainly made this worse, but there were seeds of this seclusion that had been sowed long before COVID was ever heard of.

Isolation is Not a Natural State

Looking back to the Garden of Eden we can see that Adam was created before Eve. While there were lots of animals around, there was no true companionship for Adam. And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him … And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him –Genesis 2:18-20.

And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man –Genesis 2:21-22. Of course, this was the beginning of marriage, but the more important thing to see here is that it is not a normal state for humans to be alone. We desire companionship and not just the companionship of a pet dog or cat.

Isolation can lead to Despair

Perhaps there is no story that demonstrates so clearly the dangers of isolation as the story of Elijah. We know from the biblical book of I Kings, that Elijah was a fiery prophet of God.

He brought word from God to Ahab that there would be no rain and there was terrible drought for the next three and a half years. During that time, Elijah spent time in the wilderness and then with a widow in Zarephath.

The whole time, he was miraculously fed through God’s power, first by ravens and then through God’s provision of flour and oil to a widow, with whom he lived. Through God’s power, he raised the widow’s son to life.

Then came a time when he challenged the prophets of Baal to a match on Mt. Carmel and won a decisive victory for God. Miraculous fire descended from heaven in answer to his prayer. Truly, God was working great things in his life.

Very soon though, Elijah was running for his life into the desert. Jezebel had threatened his life and rather than trusting God, he fled to Mt. Horeb where he heard the voice of God.

When God asked him what he was doing there, Elijah replied, …I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: for the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away –1 Kings 19:10.

We can see here a big reason for Elijah’s weakness. He felt completely alone. God corrected Elijah’s incorrect assumption when He stated: Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him –1 Kings 19:18.

The fact that those men and women existed in Israel did Elijah little good since he didn’t spend time with them. Elijah’s isolation led him to weakness and despair.

The story of Paul comes to mind as well. The Apostle Paul was a man who seemed to have nearly limitless amounts of energy and an unquenchable zeal for the things of God, but his last letter to Timothy from prison revealed a man who felt very alone. Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee… –2 Timothy 4:9-11.

The Apostle was not abandoned. Other than Demas, they had not fled because they were afraid or ashamed of his bonds. He had sent many of his friends away to strengthen the church in various parts of the Roman Empire. Yet, Paul was still feeling isolated and needed the good Christian brothers, Timothy and Mark, to come and encourage him as he faced a martyr’s death.

Isolation is Physically Harmful

Studies have showed that isolation is linked to higher rates of high blood pressure, heart disease, anxiety, and depression. Older people who are isolated often show signs of mental decline and can experience worsening dementia.

Many times, as people age, they experience the deaths of loved ones. The loss of a spouse can lead older people to withdraw from others and to experience loneliness and isolation. This in turn often leads to rapid progression of the aging process.

Science does not fully understand it, but loneliness leads to increased inflammation and poorer immune function. This in turn can lead to lonely people getting worse infections and struggling to recover after such an infection.

While we think of these problems as those that primarily affect elderly people, they can affect younger people as well. In younger people, often loneliness doesn’t lead to memory issues, but it certainly can lead to things like depression, and it can make chronic inflammatory diseases much worse.

The Opposite of Isolation

If asked what the opposite of isolation is most people would probably answer “Companionship” or maybe even “Friendship”. There is another word which has a Christian connotation that is even better. That word is fellowship.

The Greek word translated fellowship in the New Testament is “Koinonia” and in the Bible it speaks of relationships that are founded on a shared love for God and for the church—a unity of belief and desire. Christian fellowship includes concepts like praying together, encouraging one another, and even suffering together.

I am afraid that many today find themselves in one of two dangerous situations. First, they may not be a member of any church congregation. While this may be unavoidable in certain mission outreach situations, it is not ideal, and most certainly it should not be a normal situation. At the very least it can create a sense of isolation, and at the worst it hinders many of the “one-anothering” Bible passages from being followed. We need fellowship, both to encourage us and to keep us accountable.

The second dangerous situation is that many believers, while members of a church, isolate themselves within that church. If you are a member of a large church congregation, it is easy to blend in and not develop relationships with others. This is just as harmful as not being a member of a church body. Too many people feel lonely, even when there are lots of people around.

Scripture makes it clear that we need a church body. Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching –Hebrews 10:25.

There are many people who have lives that are full of friends and acquaintances, but if they do not have a place where they receive fellowship, they are missing out.

When I see people in my office who are struggling with depression there are two things I always tell them to do for themselves.

First is to start exercising. There have been several studies that compared exercise to antidepressants and found that it had similar effectiveness to many of the commonly prescribed antidepressant medications. This doesn’t have to be really vigorous exercise, but it does need to be aerobic (enough to raise the heart rate) and consistent.

The second is to become active in a church congregation; it is not enough to just attend church. Having brothers and sisters to pray for someone who is struggling, to listen to the discouraging situations, and to encourage that person to a more vibrant walk with God is really helpful.

Unfortunately, when someone is struggling with depression, the last thing they seem to want to do is make the effort to be around other people, which contrary to their feelings, is counterproductive to changing the problem.

As we consider this, it should move us to reach out to those who we know are struggling with isolation.

When someone loses a spouse, they often have a lot of encouragement for the first several weeks, but we need to make certain that they continue to have an active presence in their lives in the months that follow.

For every man shall bear his own burden –Galatians 6:5, should not give us excuse to not obey God’s command to Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ –Galatians 6:2. The family of God is given no time limit on bearing burdens. There is only a mandate that as we see our brother or sister struggling, we are to help them, as we are able.

The blessing is that someday, when we are struggling, we will have men and women of faith around us to encourage us and to pray for us. We cannot carry these burdens alone. Together, we will reach the Celestial City.

Isolation comes for many reasons. Sometimes it seems to be a chosen way of life, as is the natural tendency of introverted people. Sometimes it is foisted upon a person due to deaths of loved ones or other significant losses. Either way, it is not a healthy place to live.

As we find ourselves in these situations, we need to reach out for fellowship. The family of God is there for us if we only reach out.

As we see others who are struggling, we need to extend to them the right arm of fellowship. As we do so, we may, through our small efforts, help someone emotionally, physically, and spiritually, simply by being a friend in a time of isolation.

Rundt om i verden, men spesielt i USA, ser det ut til at folk verdsetter robust individualisme. Mennesker som viser denne karakteregenskapen klarer seg selv i livet, ber ikke andre om hjelp og forventer ingenting.

Jeg antar at denne ideen kan føres tilbake til pionerene. Dette var menn og kvinner som drog over nye landområder på jakt etter et sted de kunne slå seg ned og kalle hjem. Det var få landhandlere, og så langt det lot seg gjøre levde de så selvforsynt som mulig.

Selv om dette kan høres ut som et scenario som demonstrerer styrke, er sannheten noe annerledes i dag. I dag bruker folk teknologi for bevisst å skape bobler av isolasjon rundt seg.

Mange eldre har funnet seg mer og mer isolert fra venner og familie. COVID gjorde dette helt klart verre, men det var kimen til denne tilbaketrukketheten som ble sådd lenge før COVID ble kjent.

Isolasjon er ikke en naturlig tilstand

Ser vi tilbake til Edens hage kan vi se at Adam ble skapt før Eva. Selv om det fantes mange dyr omkring, var det ikke ekte fellesskap for Adam. Og Herren Gud sa: Det er ikke godt at mennesket er alene; jeg vil gjøre ham en hjelper som er hans like … Og Adam ga navn til alle husdyrene, himmelens fugler og alle markens dyr; men for Adam ble det ikke funnet noen hjelper som var hans like –Genesis 2:18-20.

Og Herren Gud fikk det til å falle en tung søvn over Adam, og han sov: og han tok et av hans ribben, og fylte igjen kjøttet i stedet for det; Og ribbenet som Herren Gud hadde tatt fra mennesket, gjorde han til en kvinne, og brakte henne til mannen –Genesis 2:21-22. Selvfølgelig var dette begynnelsen på ekteskapet, men det viktigste å se her er at det ikke er en normal tilstand for mennesker å være alene. Vi lengter etter fellesskap, og ikke bare fellesskapet med en hund eller katt.

Isolasjon kan føre til fortvilelse

Kanskje finnes det ingen historie som så klart viser farene ved isolasjon som Elia-historien. Vi vet fra det bibelske 1. Kongebok at Elia var en lidenskapelig Guds profet.

Han forkynte for Akab at det ikke ville komme regn, og det ble en forferdelig tørke i de neste tre og et halvt årene. I løpet av den tiden oppholdt Elia seg i ødemarken og senere hos en enke i Sarepta.

Gjennom hele denne tiden ble han underliggjort forsørget ved Guds makt, først av kråker og senere ved at Gud sørget for mel og olje til enken han bodde hos. Ved Guds makt oppreiste han enkens sønn til livet.

Så kom tiden da han utfordret Ba’al-profetene til dyst på Karmel og vant en avgjørende seier for Gud. Mirakuløs ild falt fra himmelen som svar på hans bønn. Sannelig, Gud gjorde store ting i hans liv.

Svært snart flyktet Elia imidlertid for livet utover i ørkenen. Jezebel hadde truet hans liv, og i stedet for å stole på Gud, flyktet han til Horeb-fjellet hvor han hørte Guds røst.

Når Gud spurte ham hva han gjorde der, svarte Elia, …jeg har vært meget nidkjær for Herren, hærskarenes Gud; for Israels barn har forkastet din pakt, revet ned dine alter og drept dine profeter med sverd; og jeg, jeg ene, er igjen; og de søker mitt liv for å ta det bort –1 Kings 19:10.

Her ser vi en viktig grunn til Elias svakhet. Han følte seg fullstendig alene. Gud rettet Elias feilaktige antagelse da Han uttalte: Men jeg har latt syv tusen være igjen i Israel, alle dem som ikke har bøyd kne for Baal, og hver munn som ikke har kysset ham –1 Kings 19:18.

Det faktum at disse mennene og kvinnene eksisterte i Israel gjorde lite for Elia siden han ikke tilbrakte tid sammen med dem. Elias isolasjon førte ham til svakhet og fortvilelse.

Paulus’ historie kommer også i tankene. Apostelen Paulus var en mann som syntes å ha nesten grenseløs energi og en ustoppelig iver for Guds ting, men hans siste brev til Timoteus fra fengselet viste en mann som følte seg veldig alene. Gjør hva du kan for å komme til meg snart: For Demas har forlatt meg, fordi han elsket denne nåværende verden, og er reist til Tessalonika; Krescens til Galatia, Titus til Dalmatia. Bare Lukas er hos meg. Ta Markus med, og bring ham med deg… –2 Timothy 4:9-11.

Apostelen var ikke forlatt. Bortsett fra Demas hadde de ikke flyktet av frykt eller skam over hans lenker. Han hadde sendt mange av vennene sine for å styrke menigheten i ulike deler av Romerriket. Likevel følte Paulus seg isolert og trengte de gode kristne brødrene Timoteus og Markus til å komme og oppmuntre ham mens han sto overfor et martyrdød.

Isolasjon er fysisk skadelig

Studier har vist at isolasjon er knyttet til høyere forekomst av høyt blodtrykk, hjertesykdom, angst og depresjon. Eldre som er isolerte viser ofte tegn til mental tilbakegang og kan oppleve forverret demens.

Mange ganger, når folk blir eldre, opplever de dødsfall blant sine kjære. Tapet av en ektefelle kan få eldre til å trekke seg unna andre og å oppleve ensomhet og isolasjon. Dette fører ofte til en raskere aldringsprosess.

Vitenskapen forstår det ikke fullt ut, men ensomhet fører til økt inflammasjon og dårligere immunfunksjon. Dette kan igjen føre til at ensomme mennesker får verre infeksjoner og har vanskeligere for å komme seg etter slike infeksjoner.

Selv om vi tenker på disse problemene som noe som primært rammer eldre, kan de også ramme yngre mennesker. Hos yngre fører ensomhet ofte ikke til hukommelsesproblemer, men det kan absolutt føre til ting som depresjon, og det kan gjøre kroniske inflammatoriske sykdommer mye verre.

Det motsatte av isolasjon

Hvis man spør hva det motsatte av isolasjon er, ville de fleste trolig svare «selskap» eller kanskje «vennskap». Det finnes et annet ord med en kristen konnotasjon som er enda bedre. Det ordet er fellesskap.

Det greske ordet som oversettes med fellesskap i Det nye testamente er «Koinonia», og i Bibelen taler det om relasjoner som er forankret i en delt kjærlighet til Gud og til kirken—en enhet i tro og ønske. Kristent fellesskap omfatter begreper som å be sammen, oppmuntre hverandre og til og med lide sammen.

Jeg er redd for at mange i dag befinner seg i en av to farlige situasjoner. For det første kan de stå uten medlemskap i noen kirkesamfunn. Selv om dette av og til kan være uunngåelig i visse misjons- eller utsendelsessituasjoner, er det ikke ideelt, og det bør absolutt ikke være en normal situasjon. I beste fall kan det skape en følelse av isolasjon, og i verste fall hindrer det mange av bibelens «hverandre»-passasjer fra å bli fulgt. Vi trenger fellesskap, både for å oppmuntre oss og for å holde oss ansvarlige.

Den andre farlige situasjonen er at mange troende, selv om de er medlemmer av en kirke, isolerer seg innenfor den kirken. Hvis du er medlem av en stor menighet, er det lett å gå i ett med mengden og ikke utvikle relasjoner med andre. Dette er like skadelig som å ikke være medlem av en kirkekropp. Altfor mange føler seg ensomme, selv når det er mange mennesker rundt dem.

Skriften gjør det klart at vi trenger en kirke. La oss ikke forlate våre sammenkomster, slik noen har for vane, men la oss oppmuntre hverandre, og det desto mer som dere ser dagen nærme seg –Hebrews 10:25.

Det finnes mange som har liv fulle av venner og bekjente, men hvis de ikke har et sted hvor de mottar fellesskap, går de glipp av noe vesentlig.

Når jeg ser mennesker på mitt kontor som sliter med depresjon, er det to ting jeg alltid sier at de må gjøre for seg selv.

Det første er å begynne å trene. Flere studier har sammenlignet trening med antidepressiva og funnet at det hadde liknende effekt som mange av de vanlig foreskrevne antidepressiva. Dette trenger ikke være svært intens trening, men det må være aerob (nok til å øke pulsen) og konsistent.

Det andre er å bli aktiv i en menighet; det er ikke nok bare å delta i gudstjenester. Å ha brødre og søstre som ber for en som strever, som lytter til nedbrytende situasjoner, og som oppmuntrer vedkommende til et mer livskraftig vandring med Gud, er virkelig hjelpsomt.

Dessverre, når noen sliter med depresjon, er det siste de ofte ønsker å gjøre å anstrenge seg for å være rundt andre mennesker, hvilket i motsetning til deres følelser er kontraproduktivt for å endre problemet.

Når vi tenker på dette, bør det få oss til å strekke oss ut til dem vi vet sliter med isolasjon.

Når noen mister en ektefelle, får de ofte mye oppmuntring de første ukene, men vi må sørge for at de fortsetter å ha en aktiv tilstedeværelse i livene sine i månedene som følger.

For hver mann skal bære sin egen byrde –Galatians 6:5, bør ikke gi oss unnskyldning for å ikke adlyde Guds befaling om å Bær hverandres byrder, og så oppfyll loven i Kristus –Galatians 6:2. Guds familie er ikke gitt noen tidsbegrensning for å bære byrder. Det er kun et påbud om at når vi ser vår bror eller søster slite, skal vi hjelpe dem etter evne.

Velsignelsen er at en dag, når vi selv sliter, vil vi ha troens menn og kvinner rundt oss til å oppmuntre oss og be for oss. Vi kan ikke bære disse byrdene alene. Sammen skal vi nå Den himmelske byen.

Isolasjon kommer av mange grunner. Noen ganger ser det ut som en valgt livsstil, slik det ofte er for innadvendte mennesker. Noen ganger påtvinges det en person på grunn av dødsfall blant kjære eller andre betydelige tap. Uansett er det ikke et sunt sted å leve.

Når vi befinner oss i slike situasjoner, må vi rekke ut etter fellesskap. Guds familie er der for oss hvis vi bare strekker ut hånden.

Når vi ser andre som sliter, må vi rekke dem den rette arm av fellesskap. Når vi gjør det, kan vi gjennom våre små anstrengelser hjelpe noen følelsesmessig, fysisk og åndelig, bare ved å være en venn i en tid med isolasjon.
